title: US Healthcare Map
summary: A plain-English map of who pays, who provides and who sits in the middle of US healthcare, plus why it costs so much. Healthcare is one of the most common US case industries, and interviewers assume you know the players.

blocks.title: The big picture
blocks.body: The US spent ~$5.3T on health in 2024, ~18% of GDP and ~$15.5K per person (CMS). There is no single payer: most working-age people are covered through an employer, older adults through Medicare, lower-income people through Medicaid, and others buy plans on the ACA marketplace. Roughly 8% of people were uninsured in 2024 (Census). Money flows through insurers and intermediaries before reaching hospitals, doctors and pharmacies.

blocks.title: Who pays: the coverage map
rows: Federal: payroll tax, premiums, general revenue
blocks.note: People can hold more than one type (e.g. Medicare + Medicaid), so shares overlap.

blocks.title: The main players
items: Providers: hospitals and health systems (~6,100 hospitals, most community hospitals nonprofit), physician groups, clinics, nursing facilities.
Payers: insurers like UnitedHealth, Elevance, Cigna, Aetna (CVS), Humana; plus government programs.
Self-insured employers: large firms often bear the claims risk and hire an insurer only to administer.
PBMs: manage drug benefits; the big three (Express Scripts, CVS Caremark, Optum Rx) handled ~80% of claims in 2025.
Manufacturers: pharma, biotech and device makers.
Vertical integration: insurers increasingly own PBMs, pharmacies and physician groups.

blocks.title: The drug channel
blocks.body: Drugs move physically from manufacturer to wholesaler (a few big distributors) to pharmacy to patient. Money moves differently. The PBM negotiates rebates from manufacturers in exchange for favorable formulary placement, builds pharmacy networks, and processes claims for the plan sponsor. List prices can rise while net prices after rebates fall, so the patient paying coinsurance on list price can lose out. That gap drives much of the PBM policy debate.

blocks.title: Why US prices are high
items: Prices per service, not usage, are the main driver: hospital stays, specialist fees and branded drugs cost more than in peer countries.
Fragmented payers mean weaker bargaining power than a single national buyer.
Hospital consolidation gives systems leverage to negotiate higher commercial rates.
Heavy administrative cost from billing across many plans with different rules.
Private insurers typically pay hospitals well above Medicare rates, cross-subsidizing public payers.

rows: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the federal agency running both
Affordable Care Act (2010), created marketplaces, expanded Medicaid
Medicare Advantage, private plans for Medicare beneficiaries

blocks.title: 'Insured' does not mean costs are covered
blocks.body: Deductibles and coinsurance are common. The average single-coverage deductible for workers was ~$1.9K in 2025, and a family employer premium averaged ~$27K (KFF). Patients still shop on price for some services, and bad debt is a real line item for hospitals.

blocks.title: Always ask about payer mix
blocks.body: For any provider case, ask what share of revenue comes from commercial, Medicare and Medicaid. Commercial pays the most, Medicaid the least. A hospital losing commercial patients can see margins collapse even if volume is flat.

in_a_case: Hospital margin case: start with payer mix and commercial rate negotiations before chasing volume; Medicaid-heavy systems run thin margins.
Pharma launch: map formulary access through the PBMs and expect rebate demands; list price is not what the manufacturer nets.
Employer benefits cost case: large employers are often self-insured, so levers include PBM contract terms, narrow networks and GLP-1 coverage policy.
Insurer growth case: Medicare Advantage is the profit pool most players fight over; watch star ratings and government reimbursement changes.
Policy shock: ACA subsidy changes or Medicaid eligibility rules shift coverage, which changes providers' uncompensated care and insurers' risk pools.
